case_name: State Of Uttar Pradesh v Devendra Singh
respondent:
Devendra Singh
Supreme Court of India

13 April 2004
Appeal (crl.) 617 of 1998
The Judgment was delivered by : Arijit Pasayat, J.
1.  The State of Uttar Pradesh in this appeal questioned the legality of the judgment rendered by Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court which set aside the conviction of the accused-respondent under Sections 302, 376 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code 1860 (in short 'IPC). The Trial Court had found the accused guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for life for the first offence, and seven years and five years for the other two offences respectively. High Court, in appeal, reversed the judgment of the Trial Court and directed acquittal.

facts: The State of Uttar Pradesh questioned the legality of the judgment rendered by Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court which set aside the conviction of the accused-respondent under Sections 302, 376 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code 1860.

Complainant Brij Lal (PW-1) was father of the deceased aged about 10 years. On 26.12.1978, at about noon, the deceased went to the 'Kolhu' of Rajendra Singh father of the accused, in order to chew sugarcane.

The complainant and some other witnesses went the next day to the sugarcane field of accused Devendra Singh in order to search for the deceased in the said field. The accused did not permit the complainant to have a look at the said sugarcane field.
During the search, some portion of the field towards the south was found to be freshly dug. The complainant and others dug the staid place and the dead body of the deceased was found buried there.
issues: Whether the High Court's approach in discarding the evidence of PW-4 is correct?
petitioner_arguments: The approach of the High Court is clearly erroneous. Merely because PW-4 who was at the relevant time about 16 years of age, and has given reasons as to why he did not disclose having seen the throttling for about three days that should not have been held sufficient to wipe out his credible evidence.
There is no record to show that he had admitted not to have seen the occurrence. It appears to be an error of record.
respondent_arguments: The High Court has rightly discarded the evidence of PW-4, finding his conduct to be unnatural. Though the record does not show it, on the first day of examination, PW-4 had stated not to have seen the occurrence.
If evidence of PW-4 is kept out of consideration, evidence of others who claimed to have seen the accused in the company of the deceased prior to the incident is of no consequence.
court_reasoning: To discard the evidence of a witness on the ground that he did not react in any particular manner is to appreciate evidence in a wholly unrealistic and unimaginative way.

The High Court erred in observing that he had stated during examination about his having not seen the occurrence and later on clarifying that he did so because of threats given by the accused. PW-4 nowhere stated of his having not seen the occurrence.
holding: The conviction as recorded by the Trial Court and the sentences imposed are restored. Accused shall surrender to custody forthwith to serve the sentence imposed by the Trial Court.
